Paragraph 1:
"Large language model inference on a single GPU is often governed less by raw floating point throughput than by the movement of tensors between high bandwidth memory and the limited on chip memory of streaming multiprocessors. During autoregressive decoding, each newly generated token requires the model to read the weights of the target network and, more importantly, to read the key and value tensors that have been accumulated for every previous token in the sequence. These key and value tensors, commonly called the KV cache, grow linearly with sequence length and batch size, and they can dominate the memory footprint of a long context inference workload. Because the arithmetic intensity of a single decode step is low, the GPU frequently spends more time waiting for data than performing useful matrix multiplications. This observation motivates a family of systems techniques that reduce redundant memory traffic, increase the amount of useful work per byte moved, and exploit the fact that modern accelerators have a deep memory hierarchy. Speculative decoding, flash attention, and KV cache traffic management are three such techniques, and they interact in subtle ways when deployed on a single GPU."

P2:
"Speculative decoding is a method for accelerating autoregressive generation by using a smaller or cheaper draft model to propose several future tokens, after which the larger target model verifies those proposals in a single forward pass. The draft model may be a separate small transformer, a pruned version of the target, a quantized copy, or even a heuristic such as n gram lookup, but the essential idea is that it can generate candidate tokens quickly. The target model then processes the original prompt together with the proposed tokens as a short prefill, producing logits for each position. By comparing the target distribution with the draft distribution, the algorithm accepts a prefix of the proposed tokens and, if necessary, samples one additional token from a corrected residual distribution.
